Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals CNC Meets 3D Printing Smarter Stainless Steel Manufacturing for Aerospace, Medical & More Published May 15, 2025, updated May 15, 2025 5 min In the high-end manufacturing industry, the complex structure of stainless steel parts and high-precision demand for the traditional manufacturing model presents a great challenge. The synergistic application of CNC machining and metal 3D printing is through the “near-net shaping + precision machining” hybrid manufacturing strategy, breakthrough technology bottlenecks, to achieve the double optimization of cost and efficiency. This article will analyze the stainless steel hybrid manufacturing technology path, core advantages and industry applications. I. Stainless steel hybrid manufacturing technology logic: 3D printing and CNC synergy optimization 1. Complementary technical characteristics 3D printing (SLM/DMLS) : The use of laser melting stainless steel powder layer by layer, can be shaped into complex cavities, lattice structure and other traditional processes difficult to achieve the geometry, the material utilization rate of up to 95%. CNC Machining: Precision cutting of 3D printed blanks through 5-axis linkage technology, surface roughness up to Ra0.4μm, tolerance control ±0.01mm, to meet the needs of high-precision assembly. 2. Hybrid manufacturing process Near-net-molding stage: Printing stainless steel blanks based on SLM technology, retaining critical area allowance (0.1-0.3mm) to reduce material waste. Precision machining stage: Five-axis CNC machine tool finishes critical areas such as mating surfaces, threaded holes, etc. to eliminate print layer pattern and optimize surface quality. Post-processing integration: Sandblasting, electrolytic polishing and other processes to enhance corrosion resistance, anodizing to enhance surface hardness (HV ≥ 800). II. 4 Core Advantages of Hybrid Manufacturing 1. Cost reduction: material and man-hours double optimization Case: an aerospace engine bracket using hybrid manufacturing, 3D printing weight reduction of 40%, CNC machining only 20% of the traditional labor hours, total cost reduction of 35%, complex parts processing cycle shortened by 50%. 2. Integrated molding of complex structures Technological breakthroughs: Conformal Cooling Runner: 3D printing embedded spiral water path, CNC finishing sealing surface, mold life increased by 3 times. Skeletonization and lightweighting: Titanium-stainless steel composite structure, unchanged strength and 50% weight reduction. 3. Synergistic improvement of precision and performance Surface quality: Hybrid manufacturing part surface roughness optimized from Ra30μm in SLM to Ra0.4μm to meet medical device implantation requirements. Mechanical properties: Tensile strength is increased by 15% (e.g. 17-4PH up to 1200MPa) through CNC elimination of printing residual stresses. 4. Small batch agile production Support 1-piece ordering, from design to delivery in as fast as 3 days (traditional mold manufacturing takes more than 30 days). III. Stainless steel hybrid manufacturing of the five innovative application direction 1. Semiconductor equipment precision components Demand: wafer transfer robotic arm needs to be both lightweight (weight reduction of 30%) and corrosion resistance (resistant to strong acid environment). Solution: 316L stainless steel 3D printed honeycomb sandwich structure, CNC finishing gripping surface, surface roughness up to Ra0.2μm, precision ± 0.005mm, life expectancy increased by 3 times. Value: a lithography manufacturer through the program, wafer transfer speed increased by 15%, maintenance cycle extended to 12 months. 2. Functional integration of energy equipment Hydrogen energy field: Fuel cell bipolar plate adopts 3D printing runner + CNC sealing surface processing, hydrogen permeability is reduced to 0.01cm³/min, and mass production cost is reduced by 40%. Nuclear energy field: nuclear reactor cooling tube by SLM molding inner wall spiral groove, 5-axis CNC polishing to Ra0.1μm, heat exchange efficiency increased by 25%. 3. Smart hardware structural innovation Consumer electronics: folding screen cell phone hinges are manufactured with 17-4PH stainless steel hybrid, realizing 0.01mm-level assembly tolerance and opening and closing life of over 500,000 times. Robot joints: Many robot joints use 3D-printed bionic bone structure, and then use CNC machining their bearing mating surfaces, so that the dynamic load capacity of the robot joints is increased by 30% and the weight is reduced by 40%. 4. Green Circular Economy Practices Waste material regeneration: remelting stainless steel scraps from CNC machining into 3D printing powder, material utilization rate increased from 20% to 95%. Low-carbon process: hybrid manufacturing energy consumption is 60% lower than traditional casting, and an enterprise reduces carbon emissions by 1,200 tons per year. IV. 3 Implementation Strategies for Hybrid Manufacturing 1. Material and process matching Material selection: Prioritize 316L or 17-4PH stainless steel with strong SLM suitability to avoid work hardening. Parameter synergy: Printing layer thickness: 20-40μm (balance efficiency and surface quality). Cutting parameters: carbide tool line speed 80-120m/min, feed 0.05mm/tooth. 2. Digital full-process management Software integration: UG/NX and other platforms to achieve “modeling - slicing - machining path” integrated programming, reducing data conversion errors. Intelligent inspection: Combination of coordinate measurement (CMM) and CT scanning ensures that the detection rate of internal defects is >99%. 3. Economic assessment model Cost formula: Total Cost = Printing Cost (Material + Energy) + CNC Finishing Cost (Man-hour + Tool) When the complexity of the part > 60%, the cost of the hybrid program is lower than pure CNC machining. V. Introduction: The importance of understanding CNC machining misconceptions CNC (Computer Numerical Control) machining has become an integral part of the modern manufacturing industry and is widely used in a variety of fields due to its high accuracy and efficiency. From automotive to aerospace, from medical to electronics, CNC machining technology provides manufacturers with a wealth of machining solutions. However, in practice, some common misconceptions often affect machining accuracy, productivity and the quality of the final product. This article will explore these common misconceptions and provide solutions to help manufacturers avoid problems that may arise in CNC machining, and enhance production levels. II. Common misconceptions about CNC machining 1. Excessive pursuit of machining accuracy In many CNC machining projects, the excessive pursuit of very high precision often leads to unnecessary machining difficulties and cost increases. While high-precision machining is critical in certain demanding industries, in many cases, overly tight tolerance requirements not only increase manufacturing time, but can also lead to rapid tool wear. How to avoid it: Set tolerances appropriately and consider the actual use of the part. If the function of the part does not require extreme accuracy, tolerances can be relaxed appropriately, reducing machining costs and increasing productivity. Example: For example, in the mass production of automotive parts, excessive pursuit of micron-level tolerances may lead to unnecessary machining processes. By setting tolerances to a reasonable range, the functionality of the part can be ensured and significant savings in machining time and cost can be achieved. 2. Inappropriate material selection Selection of unsuitable materials often leads to increased machining difficulty and even increased tool wear during machining, reducing productivity. Material selection is critical to the CNC machining process, and the hardness, toughness, thermal conductivity and wear resistance of different materials have a significant impact on the machining process. How to avoid: Select materials based on the functional requirements, mechanical properties and machining characteristics of the part. Designers should communicate with CNC machining suppliers to understand the impact of material properties on the machining process and make a reasonable choice. Example: For example, aluminium alloys are suitable for parts with lightweight requirements, but for parts that need to withstand large mechanical loads, using steel or titanium alloys may be more appropriate. Selecting materials according to different needs can effectively avoid difficulties and mistakes in machining. 3. Neglect tool selection and maintenance Tool selection and maintenance for CNC machining is critical. Inappropriate tool selection may lead to errors in the machining process, or even cause parts to be scrapped. Tool wear, deformation and other problems are also common misconceptions in machining. How to avoid: Select the appropriate tool according to the machining material, part shape and machining accuracy requirements, and regularly check the wear of the tool. Replace the tool in time to maintain the sharpness of the tool to ensure the smoothness of the machining process. Example illustration: In the machining of complex parts, failure to replace or maintain tools in a timely manner may result in substandard accuracy or even damage to machining equipment. Regularly check the condition of the tool and adjust it according to the machining needs. 4. Design does not take into account the actual limitations of the machining process Many designers ignore the actual limitations of CNC machining in the design stage, such as machining angle, fixture positioning and other issues, resulting in an infeasible design or difficult machining. Designs that do not take machining constraints into account can lead to extensive corrections and redesigns. How to avoid it: Designers should be aware of the process limitations of CNC machining and fully consider the problems that may be encountered in practice. Communicate with the CNC machining service provider during the design phase to ensure that the design meets the machining requirements. Example: When designing a complex part that requires multiple machining angles, this may not be possible due to the limitations of the machining machine. Therefore, the actual machinable range of the machine should be considered during design to avoid overly complex designs. 5. Improper setting of cutting speed and feed rate Cutting speed and feed rate settings directly affect the efficiency and accuracy of machining. If the settings are not appropriate, not only will reduce the processing efficiency, but also may have an impact on the quality of the parts, and even lead to damage to the processing equipment. How to avoid: Set a reasonable cutting speed and feed rate according to the characteristics of the machined material, the type of tool and the capability of the machining equipment. Through accurate calculation, adjust the feed rate to improve machining efficiency and ensure the quality of machining. Example illustration: For materials with high hardness, such as stainless steel, too high cutting speed may lead to excessive tool wear or even machining failure. Reasonable cutting parameters can extend tool life and improve productivity. 6. Ignoring subsequent machining requirements Some of the pitfalls in CNC machining stem from a failure to consider subsequent machining requirements at the design stage. For example, some designs may not take into account surface treatments, heat treatments, or other subsequent processes, resulting in a failure to progress to the next process. How to avoid: Subsequent processing needs of the part should be fully considered during the design process to ensure that the design can support subsequent process steps. Maintain communication with the machining service provider and subsequent processing vendors to ensure the entire process runs smoothly. Example: For example, when designing a precision mechanical part, failure to consider subsequent heat treatment needs may result in deformation or insufficient hardness of the part after machining, affecting the final performance of the product. Planning the subsequent treatment process in advance is the key to avoiding misunderstandings. III. How to avoid the misunderstanding in CNC machining 1. Effective communication and collaboration at the design stage Effective communication between designers and CNC machining suppliers is crucial to avoiding misunderstandings. By working with engineers, designers are able to understand the problems that may be encountered during the machining process and optimise the design. 2. Simulation with advanced CNC technology and software Modern CAD/CAM software can virtually simulate a design to help designers identify possible machining problems. By simulating the machining process, designers can make adjustments in advance to avoid mistakes in the actual machining. 3. Optimise the production process By optimising the production process, selecting the appropriate processing path and operation steps, it can reduce processing time and improve production efficiency. At the same time, rational arrangement of the processing sequence to avoid redundant operations. 4. Regular equipment maintenance and tool inspection Regular maintenance of CNC equipment and tools to ensure that the equipment is in the best working condition. Use the intelligent monitoring system to check the operating condition of the equipment in real time, prevent potential failures and ensure smooth processing. IV. Advantages of JLCCNC: The Best Partner to Avoid Common Misconceptions JLCCNC provides customers with a full range of services from design to processing, to ensure that each processing meets high standards. Our precision equipment and technical team can help customers to avoid possible misunderstandings in the machining process, so as to improve product quality and production efficiency. Precision design and machining synergy: JLCCNC works closely with our customers to provide machining feasibility assessments during the design phase to ensure a high degree of design-machining synergy. High Precision and High Performance Equipment: We use advanced CNC equipment and technology to meet a variety of precision machining needs, ensuring machining accuracy and productivity. Professional Technical Team: JLCCNC has an experienced technical team, which is able to find and solve any problems in the processing in a timely manner, providing customers with efficient and high-quality processing services. V. Conclusion Avoiding common CNC machining mistakes is essential to improve machining quality, reduce production costs and shorten delivery time. Introduction: The importance of understanding CNC machining misconceptions CNC (Computer Numerical Control) machining has become an integral part of the modern manufacturing industry and is widely used in a variety of fields due to its high accuracy and efficiency. From automotive to aerospace, from medical to electronics, CNC machining technology provides manufacturers with a wealth of machining solutions. However, in practice, some common misconceptions often affect machining accuracy, productivity and the quality of the final product. This article will explore these common misconceptions and provide solutions to help manufacturers avoid problems that may arise in CNC machining, and enhance production levels. II. Common misconceptions about CNC machining 1. Excessive pursuit of machining accuracy In many CNC machining projects, the excessive pursuit of very high precision often leads to unnecessary machining difficulties and cost increases. While high-precision machining is critical in certain demanding industries, in many cases, overly tight tolerance requirements not only increase manufacturing time, but can also lead to rapid tool wear. How to avoid it: Set tolerances appropriately and consider the actual use of the part. If the function of the part does not require extreme accuracy, tolerances can be relaxed appropriately, reducing machining costs and increasing productivity. Example: For example, in the mass production of automotive parts, excessive pursuit of micron-level tolerances may lead to unnecessary machining processes. By setting tolerances to a reasonable range, the functionality of the part can be ensured and significant savings in machining time and cost can be achieved. 2. Inappropriate material selection Selection of unsuitable materials often leads to increased machining difficulty and even increased tool wear during machining, reducing productivity. Material selection is critical to the CNC machining process, and the hardness, toughness, thermal conductivity and wear resistance of different materials have a significant impact on the machining process. How to avoid: Select materials based on the functional requirements, mechanical properties and machining characteristics of the part. Designers should communicate with CNC machining suppliers to understand the impact of material properties on the machining process and make a reasonable choice. Example: For example, aluminium alloys are suitable for parts with lightweight requirements, but for parts that need to withstand large mechanical loads, using steel or titanium alloys may be more appropriate. Selecting materials according to different needs can effectively avoid difficulties and mistakes in machining. 3. Neglect tool selection and maintenance Tool selection and maintenance for CNC machining is critical. Inappropriate tool selection may lead to errors in the machining process, or even cause parts to be scrapped. Tool wear, deformation and other problems are also common misconceptions in machining. How to avoid: Select the appropriate tool according to the machining material, part shape and machining accuracy requirements, and regularly check the wear of the tool. Replace the tool in time to maintain the sharpness of the tool to ensure the smoothness of the machining process. Example illustration: In the machining of complex parts, failure to replace or maintain tools in a timely manner may result in substandard accuracy or even damage to machining equipment. Regularly check the condition of the tool and adjust it according to the machining needs. 4. Design does not take into account the actual limitations of the machining process Many designers ignore the actual limitations of CNC machining in the design stage, such as machining angle, fixture positioning and other issues, resulting in an infeasible design or difficult machining. Designs that do not take machining constraints into account can lead to extensive corrections and redesigns. How to avoid it: Designers should be aware of the process limitations of CNC machining and fully consider the problems that may be encountered in practice. Communicate with the CNC machining service provider during the design phase to ensure that the design meets the machining requirements. Example: When designing a complex part that requires multiple machining angles, this may not be possible due to the limitations of the machining machine. Therefore, the actual machinable range of the machine should be considered during design to avoid overly complex designs. 5. Improper setting of cutting speed and feed rate Cutting speed and feed rate settings directly affect the efficiency and accuracy of machining. If the settings are not appropriate, not only will reduce the processing efficiency, but also may have an impact on the quality of the parts, and even lead to damage to the processing equipment. How to avoid: Set a reasonable cutting speed and feed rate according to the characteristics of the machined material, the type of tool and the capability of the machining equipment. Through accurate calculation, adjust the feed rate to improve machining efficiency and ensure the quality of machining. Example illustration: For materials with high hardness, such as stainless steel, too high cutting speed may lead to excessive tool wear or even machining failure. Reasonable cutting parameters can extend tool life and improve productivity. 6. Ignoring subsequent machining requirements Some of the pitfalls in CNC machining stem from a failure to consider subsequent machining requirements at the design stage. For example, some designs may not take into account surface treatments, heat treatments, or other subsequent processes, resulting in a failure to progress to the next process. How to avoid: Subsequent processing needs of the part should be fully considered during the design process to ensure that the design can support subsequent process steps. Maintain communication with the machining service provider and subsequent processing vendors to ensure the entire process runs smoothly. Example: For example, when designing a precision mechanical part, failure to consider subsequent heat treatment needs may result in deformation or insufficient hardness of the part after machining, affecting the final performance of the product. Planning the subsequent treatment process in advance is the key to avoiding misunderstandings. III. How to avoid the misunderstanding in CNC machining 1. Effective communication and collaboration at the design stage Effective communication between designers and CNC machining suppliers is crucial to avoiding misunderstandings. By working with engineers, designers are able to understand the problems that may be encountered during the machining process and optimise the design. 2. Simulation with advanced CNC technology and software Modern CAD/CAM software can virtually simulate a design to help designers identify possible machining problems. By simulating the machining process, designers can make adjustments in advance to avoid mistakes in the actual machining. 3. Optimise the production process By optimising the production process, selecting the appropriate processing path and operation steps, it can reduce processing time and improve production efficiency. At the same time, rational arrangement of the processing sequence to avoid redundant operations. 4. Regular equipment maintenance and tool inspection Regular maintenance of CNC equipment and tools to ensure that the equipment is in the best working condition. Use the intelligent monitoring system to check the operating condition of the equipment in real time, prevent potential failures and ensure smooth processing. IV. Advantages of JLCCNC: The Best Partner to Avoid Common Misconceptions JLCCNC provides customers with a full range of services from design to processing, to ensure that each processing meets high standards. Our precision equipment and technical team can help customers to avoid possible misunderstandings in the machining process, so as to improve product quality and production efficiency. Precision design and machining synergy: JLCCNC works closely with our customers to provide machining feasibility assessments during the design phase to ensure a high degree of design-machining synergy. High Precision and High Performance Equipment: We use advanced CNC equipment and technology to meet a variety of precision machining needs, ensuring machining accuracy and productivity. Professional Technical Team: JLCCNC has an experienced technical team, which is able to find and solve any problems in the processing in a timely manner, providing customers with efficient and high-quality processing services. V. Conclusion Avoiding common CNC machining mistakes is essential to improve machining quality, reduce production costs and shorten delivery time. By setting machining parameters appropriately, optimising design and choosing the right materials, manufacturers can avoid unnecessary pitfalls and improve overall productivity. Working with a professional CNC machining service provider ensures that every aspect of the machining process meets high standards and avoids potential problems, thus improving product quality and production efficiency. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals Understanding CNC Machining Tolerances: Why They Matter for Precision Projects Published Jan 10, 2025, updated Feb 08, 2025 6 min CNC (Computer Numerical Control) machining is widely valued for its ability to produce parts with high precision and consistency. Whether it’s for a small batch of custom parts or large-scale industrial production, one of the key factors that determines the success of a CNC machining project is tolerance. In manufacturing, tolerance refers to the allowable variation in the dimensions and shape of a part. Even with the most advanced CNC machines, parts can still deviate slightly from the intended specifications. Understanding and managing these tolerances is crucial for ensuring the accuracy and quality of the final product, especially in industries where high precision is a must. In this article, we’ll take a closer look at what CNC machining tolerances are, why they’re important, and how they affect the production of high-precision parts. 1. Tolerances in CNC Machining: What Are They? The tolerance in CNC machining refers to the allowable deviation range of the part size during the machining process, that is, the allowable error between the finished product size and the designed size. Strict tolerance control can ensure the function and assembly accuracy of the parts so that their use in equipment, tools, or components can meet the expected requirements. For instance, a CNC machined part that is defined to be 100 mm long with a tolerance of ±0.1 mm can be anywhere between 99.9 mm and 100.1 mm in length and still meet the requirements. There are two primary types of tolerances in CNC machining: · Dimensional Tolerances: These define the acceptable variation in the size of a feature, such as length, width, or diameter. · Geometric Tolerances: These address the shape, form, orientation, and location of features on the part. Geometric tolerances are especially important for parts with complex features, where it’s not just the size but also the shape and position that need to be accurate. 2. Why CNC Machining Tolerances Are Crucial for Precision Projects In numerous industries, including electronics, medical devices, automotive, and aerospace, precision is essential. Poor fit, decreased functioning, or even the failure of the final assembly are just a few of the issues that can arise from a part that does not satisfy the required tolerances. Tolerances in CNC machining are crucial for precise projects for the following reasons: Provides Part Fit and Functionality: In general, precise assembly necessitates that the components fit together exactly. One component that is too large or little could negatively impact the system's overall performance. For instance, in order to ensure proper operation and safety, parts in the automotive and aircraft industries must fit tightly. Minimizes Assembly Issues: When parts are built with tight tolerances, they are less likely to cause issues during assembly. Excessive departure from a component's tolerance limits may need rework or result in delays, both of which would increase costs. Enhances Product Lifespan: Longer-lasting parts are often those manufactured within their appropriate tolerances. For example, when producing mechanical components, if one misaligned part fails because of tolerance problems, it may cause further wear or damage to nearby components. Reduces Scrap and Waste: When parts are machined to precise tolerances, they are more likely to meet the design specifications right away, reducing the need for rework or scrapping parts that don't meet standards. This helps save time and material costs. 3. The Challenges of Achieving Tight Tolerances in CNC Machining Even though CNC machines can achieve extremely tight tolerances, it can be difficult to do so reliably. Numerous elements that can affect the final product dimensions must be carefully considered in order to achieve high precision. These consist of: Machine Accuracy: The first and most crucial element is the CNC machine's own precision. Though even the best CNC machines have limitations, higher-end models are made to maintain tighter tolerances. To guarantee accuracy, the machine's calibration and maintenance must also be up to grade. Tool Wear and Condition: Over time, cutting tools wear down, which can affect the part’s dimensional accuracy. Regular monitoring of tool wear and replacement is essential to maintain tight tolerances. Material Properties: The material being machined can also affect tolerance. Materials like metals and plastics may expand or contract due to heat generated during the machining process, so adjustments need to be made to account for material behavior. Environmental Factors: Temperature fluctuations, humidity, and vibrations from surrounding machinery can all impact the CNC machining process, potentially leading to deviations in part dimensions. Many high-precision machining environments are temperature-controlled to mitigate these risks. Operator Skill: Even though CNC machines are automated, operator experience and skill are still crucial. The operator’s ability to set up the machine correctly, adjust machining parameters, and troubleshoot issues can make a significant difference in achieving the desired tolerances. 4. How to Choose the Right Tolerance for Your CNC Project Tolerances that are both reasonable and suitable for the intended use should be specified when organizing a CNC machining job. Selecting too tight tolerances might result in more expenses, longer lead times, and more challenges in reaching the intended outcomes. The following advice will help you choose the appropriate tolerance for your project: Understand the Function of the Part: Consider how the part will be used and whether the specified tolerance is truly necessary. For example, a part that doesn’t require high precision for fitment may not need tight tolerances, allowing you to save on production costs. Consult with Your CNC Manufacturer: Work closely with your CNC machining provider to determine what tolerances are achievable for the chosen material and process. Manufacturers with experience will be able to advise on the most efficient tolerance range for your specific needs. Balance Cost and Precision: Achieving tighter tolerances usually requires more advanced equipment, more time, and potentially more expensive materials. Make sure the benefits of a tighter tolerance justify the additional costs. 5. How JLCCNC Uses CNC Machining Tolerances to Guarantee Precision Delivering high-quality products is our first priority at JLCCNC, and we do this by using cutting-edge CNC machines that can achieve dependable tolerances across a variety of materials. To guarantee that every stage of the machining process satisfies exacting quality standards, our knowledgeable operators and engineers employ precision measurement instruments such as coordinate measuring machines (CMM). We provide specialized solutions for every project, whether it comprises straightforward components or more intricate geometries, because we recognize how important it is to strike a balance between cost and performance. Focusing on efficiency and cost-effectiveness, we make sure your parts fulfill the necessary requirements while optimizing production time and expenses for your projects requiring precision. Conclusion Tolerances in CNC machining are essential for guaranteeing that components are manufactured with the functionality and accuracy required for dependable, high-quality final products. You can accomplish your precision objectives while minimizing expenses and lead times by comprehending the significance of tolerances and collaborating effectively with a skilled CNC machining supplier like JLCCNC. You can guarantee that your products will fulfill the highest requirements for quality and performance by taking the proper approach to CNC machining tolerances. Understanding and managing these tolerances is crucial for ensuring the accuracy and quality of the final product, especially in industries where high precision is a must. In this article, we’ll take a closer look at what CNC machining tolerances are, why they’re important, and how they affect the production of high-precision parts. 1. Tolerances in CNC Machining: What Are They? The tolerance in CNC machining refers to the allowable deviation range of the part size during the machining process, that is, the allowable error between the finished product size and the designed size. Strict tolerance control can ensure the function and assembly accuracy of the parts so that their use in equipment, tools, or components can meet the expected requirements. For instance, a CNC machined part that is defined to be 100 mm long with a tolerance of ±0.1 mm can be anywhere between 99.9 mm and 100.1 mm in length and still meet the requirements. There are two primary types of tolerances in CNC machining: · Dimensional Tolerances: These define the acceptable variation in the size of a feature, such as length, width, or diameter. · Geometric Tolerances: These address the shape, form, orientation, and location of features on the part. Geometric tolerances are especially important for parts with complex features, where it’s not just the size but also the shape and position that need to be accurate. 2. Why CNC Machining Tolerances Are Crucial for Precision Projects In numerous industries, including electronics, medical devices, automotive, and aerospace, precision is essential. Poor fit, decreased functioning, or even the failure of the final assembly are just a few of the issues that can arise from a part that does not satisfy the required tolerances. Tolerances in CNC machining are crucial for precise projects for the following reasons: Provides Part Fit and Functionality: In general, precise assembly necessitates that the components fit together exactly. One component that is too large or little could negatively impact the system's overall performance. For instance, in order to ensure proper operation and safety, parts in the automotive and aircraft industries must fit tightly. Minimizes Assembly Issues: When parts are built with tight tolerances, they are less likely to cause issues during assembly. Excessive departure from a component's tolerance limits may need rework or result in delays, both of which would increase costs. Enhances Product Lifespan: Longer-lasting parts are often those manufactured within their appropriate tolerances. For example, when producing mechanical components, if one misaligned part fails because of tolerance problems, it may cause further wear or damage to nearby components. Reduces Scrap and Waste: When parts are machined to precise tolerances, they are more likely to meet the design specifications right away, reducing the need for rework or scrapping parts that don't meet standards. This helps save time and material costs. 3. The Challenges of Achieving Tight Tolerances in CNC Machining Even though CNC machines can achieve extremely tight tolerances, it can be difficult to do so reliably. Numerous elements that can affect the final product dimensions must be carefully considered in order to achieve high precision. These consist of: Machine Accuracy: The first and most crucial element is the CNC machine's own precision. Though even the best CNC machines have limitations, higher-end models are made to maintain tighter tolerances. To guarantee accuracy, the machine's calibration and maintenance must also be up to grade. Tool Wear and Condition: Over time, cutting tools wear down, which can affect the part’s dimensional accuracy. Regular monitoring of tool wear and replacement is essential to maintain tight tolerances. Material Properties: The material being machined can also affect tolerance. Materials like metals and plastics may expand or contract due to heat generated during the machining process, so adjustments need to be made to account for material behavior. Environmental Factors: Temperature fluctuations, humidity, and vibrations from surrounding machinery can all impact the CNC machining process, potentially leading to deviations in part dimensions. Many high-precision machining environments are temperature-controlled to mitigate these risks. Operator Skill: Even though CNC machines are automated, operator experience and skill are still crucial. The operator’s ability to set up the machine correctly, adjust machining parameters, and troubleshoot issues can make a significant difference in achieving the desired tolerances. 4. How to Choose the Right Tolerance for Your CNC Project Tolerances that are both reasonable and suitable for the intended use should be specified when organizing a CNC machining job. Selecting too tight tolerances might result in more expenses, longer lead times, and more challenges in reaching the intended outcomes. The following advice will help you choose the appropriate tolerance for your project: Understand the Function of the Part: Consider how the part will be used and whether the specified tolerance is truly necessary. For example, a part that doesn’t require high precision for fitment may not need tight tolerances, allowing you to save on production costs. Consult with Your CNC Manufacturer: Work closely with your CNC machining provider to determine what tolerances are achievable for the chosen material and process. Manufacturers with experience will be able to advise on the most efficient tolerance range for your specific needs. Balance Cost and Precision: Achieving tighter tolerances usually requires more advanced equipment, more time, and potentially more expensive materials. Make sure the benefits of a tighter tolerance justify the additional costs. 5. How JLCCNC Uses CNC Machining Tolerances to Guarantee Precision Delivering high-quality products is our first priority at JLCCNC, and we do this by using cutting-edge CNC machines that can achieve dependable tolerances across a variety of materials. To guarantee that every stage of the machining process satisfies exacting quality standards, our knowledgeable operators and engineers employ precision measurement instruments such as coordinate measuring machines (CMM). We provide specialized solutions for every project, whether it comprises straightforward components or more intricate geometries, because we recognize how important it is to strike a balance between cost and performance. Focusing on efficiency and cost-effectiveness, we make sure your parts fulfill the necessary requirements while optimizing production time and expenses for your projects requiring precision. Conclusion Tolerances in CNC machining are essential for guaranteeing that components are manufactured with the functionality and accuracy required for dependable, high-quality final products. You can accomplish your precision objectives while minimizing expenses and lead times by comprehending the significance of tolerances and collaborating effectively with a skilled CNC machining supplier like JLCCNC. You can guarantee that your products will fulfill the highest requirements for quality and performance by taking the proper approach to CNC machining tolerances. Limitations to Consider EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way Drilling a hole sounds simple, until you need to do it with extreme precision, into hardened materials, or to microscopic depths. That’s when you start comparing EDM hole drilling and conventional CNC drilling side by side. While both are designed to create holes, their technologies, capabilities, and ideal use cases couldn’t be more different. So, which method should you choose for your next project? Let’s dig in. What Is EDM Hole Drilling? EDM (Electrical Discharge Machining) hole drilling , also called hole popping EDM or EDM deep hole drilling , uses electrical sparks to erode material. Instead of a rotating drill bit, it uses a tubular electrode and dielectric fluid to remove metal through high-frequency discharges. It’s a non-contact process, meaning the tool doesn’t make direct physical contact with the material during machining. The result? It can drill extremely precise, burr-free holes even in hardened steel, carbides, or exotic alloys . What Is Conventional CNC Hole Drilling? CNC hole drilling uses rotating cutting tools<dynamic-value> twist drills or end mills, to cut into material. It's what most people imagine when they think about machining a hole. From high-speed spindles to peck drilling cycles, CNC machines are versatile and fast, especially when you're working with softer materials or mass production. But it’s still a contact-based process , and precision can degrade with wear, heat, or vibration. EDM vs Drilling: The Core Differences Feature EDM Hole Drilling CNC Drilling Material Type Conductive materials only (e.g., steel, titanium) Any machinable material Tool Contact No physical contact Direct contact via tool Hole Size Micro to medium (0.1 mm to 6 mm) Wide range (0.5 mm to 50+ mm) Tolerance Extremely tight (±0.002 mm possible) Moderate (±0.05 mm typical) Hole Depth Excellent for deep, narrow holes (30:1+ depth-to-diameter) Limited by tool rigidity and chip evacuation Speed Slower Faster for larger holes Surface Finish Very smooth, no burrs May require deburring or finishing Tool Wear Minimal due to no mechanical contact High, especially in hard materials Are you unsure about which process is right for your metal part? We can help you choose the most precise and cost-effective method for your job. Get a free quote here and let's make your design manufacturable. When to Use EDM Hole Drilling The EDM hole drilling process shines in high-precision, small-diameter, deep-hole situations, especially where conventional drilling fails or causes tool breakage. Use cases include: ● Turbine blades (for cooling holes) ● Fuel injector nozzles ● Aerospace components ● Medical devices requiring micro holes ● Hard tool steels or materials like Inconel and titanium Also, EDM is ideal when you need starter holes for wire EDM , which conventional tools can’t drill due to hardness or geometry. When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling For general-purpose hole making in aluminum, plastics, or mild steel, CNC hole drilling is faster and more cost-effective. Use cases include: ● Bolt holes, pilot holes, tapped holes ● Large hole drilling in brackets or frames ● Machining production parts in batches ● Applications where tight tolerance is not critical And yes, to answer a common question, can a CNC machine drill holes? Absolutely. In fact, it’s one of the most common operations in any CNC shop. EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? EDM holes tend to be cleaner and burr-free straight off the machine. Their surface finish is smoother, with no mechanical stress or deformation around the hole. This makes them ideal for critical applications where dimensional stability and fatigue resistance matter. CNC-drilled holes, on the other hand, often need secondary processes , like deburring or reaming, to meet similar tolerances and finishes, especially in small diameters or deep holes. Limitations to Consider While EDM hole drilling offers unmatched precision, it’s not ideal for every scenario . ● It can’t be used on non-conductive materials (like plastic or glass). ● It’s relatively slow for large-diameter holes. ● Machines and electrodes are more expensive and require specialized operators. Conversely, CNC drilling tools wear faster in hardened materials, and the deeper you go, the higher the risk of tool deflection, chatter, or breakage . EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? A dedicated hole drilling EDM machine is typically compact, automated, and capable of producing holes as small as 0.1 mm in tough metals. Many come with automatic electrode changers and multi-axis positioning. For shops working with aerospace, mold making, or die sinking, having one on the floor is a game-changer for precision parts. Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way If you're prototyping intricate components or producing parts where one imperfect hole can ruin the entire build , go for EDM. But if you’re running production batches, drilling aluminum brackets, or cutting costs, CNC drilling is often more practical. Choose the Right Tool for the Hole Not every hole is created equal, and neither are the tools that make them. Whether you choose EDM hole drilling for ultra-precision or CNC hole drilling for speed and efficiency, understanding their strengths is the first step toward better manufacturing outcomes. If you’re unsure what your application calls for, talk to your machinist, or even better, partner with a shop that offers both options . Verify Now Blog > 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling by: Mila Sep 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor 0402 capacitor 0603 capacitor 0402 vs 0603 capacitor A common misconception is that a larger capacitor package stores more energy and therefore provides better filtering performance. However, in high-speed PCB designs such as FPGA, SoC, and DDR applications, 0402 capacitors with a typical value of 0.1 μF are commonly placed near BGA core power pins instead of larger 0603 capacitors. For the same nominal capacitance, the key difference in 0402 vs 0603 capacitor performance is not how much charge the capacitor stores, but its equivalent series inductance (ESL). At lower frequencies, the performance difference between package sizes is usually less significant. As the operating frequency enters the MHz range and above, ESL increasingly affects the impedance and effective frequency range of a decoupling capacitor. The Underlying Principle: Equivalent Series Inductance (ESL) A surface-mount capacitor is not an ideal capacitor. Its equivalent circuit typically consists of an ideal capacitance (C), equivalent series resistance (ESR), and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL comes from the entire current path, including the internal electrodes, terminations, PCB pads, traces, and power/ground vias. Inductance opposes rapidly changing current, and its effect becomes more significant as frequency increases. Every capacitor has a self-resonant frequency (SRF): Operating frequency < SRF: The device behaves mainly as a capacitor and can perform its decoupling function normally. Operating frequency > SRF: The device gradually becomes inductive, and its high-frequency decoupling capability decreases. A higher self-resonant frequency generally means that a decoupling capacitor can maintain low impedance over a wider high-frequency range. For example, consider 0402 and 0603 capacitors with the same nominal capacitance of 0.1 μF: 0603 capacitor: Its larger body size generally results in a longer internal current path and higher intrinsic parasitic inductance. 0402 capacitor: Its smaller body size generally provides a shorter current path and lower intrinsic parasitic inductance. Therefore, under similar capacitance and component structures, a 0402 capacitor typically has lower parasitic inductance and a higher self-resonant frequency than a 0603 capacitor, making it more suitable for high-frequency decoupling. The actual ESL and SRF values should be verified from the component datasheet or the manufacturer's high-frequency model. PCB Pads and Vias Also Add Parasitic Inductance Engineers often focus only on the capacitor's intrinsic ESL specified in the datasheet. However, in a complete power delivery network, PCB pads, traces, and vias also introduce parasitic inductance and can sometimes have an even greater impact than the capacitor itself. In an 0402 vs 0603 capacitor comparison, the larger pads and spacing of a 0603 package can make the connection between the capacitor and power/ground vias longer. This additional trace length increases the total loop inductance. The smaller pads of a 0402 capacitor make it easier to place power and ground vias close to the component. When the PCB manufacturing and assembly processes allow it, microvias or Via-in-Pad can also be used to further shorten the current path and reduce the power-to-ground loop area. When an IC core suddenly draws high-frequency transient current, the total inductance of the current loop affects the power response. Even a capacitor with excellent electrical characteristics may provide limited high-frequency decoupling if the current path is too long. This is why the key advantage of a 0402 capacitor is not simply its smaller package size, but its ability to help create a smaller and lower-inductance current loop. （Optimized Layout） 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor: Advantages and Limitations Advantages of 0402 Capacitors Lower intrinsic parasitic inductance and typically higher SRF, providing better performance for high-frequency decoupling; Smaller pads allow the capacitor to be placed closer to BGA power pins and return paths, reducing the power-to-ground loop area; Higher placement density allows more decoupling capacitors to be placed around BGA devices, helping optimize PDN impedance; The smaller package makes it easier to implement compact power and ground via arrangements and, when supported by the PCB process, microvia or Via-in-Pad structures. Limitations of 0402 Capacitors In the same component series, the available capacitance and voltage-rating options may be more limited, while the actual effective capacitance can also decrease under DC bias; For the same capacitance and voltage rating, the component cost may be higher than that of a 0603 capacitor; Manual soldering is more difficult, with a higher risk of insufficient soldering or component loss, and mass production requires tighter stencil and placement process control; At relatively low frequencies, the performance difference between 0402 and 0603 is usually small, so a 0402 capacitor does not need to be selected simply because it is smaller. When to Use 0603 Capacitors They can generally provide sufficient performance in lower-frequency filtering applications; The larger package can make it easier to obtain suitable capacitance, voltage ratings, and mechanical reliability; They are easier to solder manually and can be suitable for general power filtering and decoupling applications where high-frequency performance is not the primary concern. Therefore, the choice between an 0402 vs 0603 capacitor should not be based on a fixed frequency boundary. As frequency increases, the ESL differences introduced by the component package and PCB mounting structure become increasingly important. The actual selection should consider effective capacitance, ESR, ESL, SRF, and the PCB layout together. Key Considerations for Decoupling Capacitor Selection and Layout Place decoupling capacitors as close as possible to BGA core power pins and other power pins that require high-frequency transient current. A 0402 capacitor is often preferred for these applications. The goal is to reduce the total parasitic inductance of the current loop and improve high-frequency PDN impedance. For DC-DC outputs and other applications where mounting inductance is less critical, 0603 or even 0805 packages can be selected according to effective capacitance, voltage rating, cost, and manufacturing requirements. Loop area is more important than package size alone. This is a common misconception in PCB decoupling. A 0402 capacitor placed far away from the IC power and return path may provide poorer high-frequency performance than a 0603 capacitor placed directly along the current path. Package size is only one factor affecting parasitic inductance. The total power-to-ground loop inductance is more important. Component placement, pad design, and via location all play an important role in PCB decoupling. Do not blindly move to a 0201 package. As the package becomes smaller, the reduction in ESL can provide diminishing returns because the PCB mounting structure can become a larger part of the total inductance. At the same time, soldering difficulty, placement requirements, and component costs may increase. A 0402 capacitor is therefore a common balance between performance, board space, and manufacturing cost in many high-speed PDN designs, although the final package should always be selected according to the specific device and manufacturing process. Common Misconceptions About Decoupling Capacitors ❌ Misconception 1: A larger capacitor package stores more energy and therefore provides better decoupling. ✅ Reality: Under the same effective capacitance and operating conditions, package size itself does not determine how much energy a capacitor stores. The high-frequency performance difference between an 0402 capacitor and a 0603 capacitor mainly comes from parasitic parameters associated with the capacitor and its PCB mounting structure, with ESL being an important factor. ❌ Misconception 2: If the capacitance is the same, the package does not matter. ✅ Reality: Even with the same nominal capacitance, different packages can have different ESL, ESR, and SRF characteristics. During decoupling capacitor selection and PDN impedance simulation, models that match the actual component and PCB mounting structure should be used whenever possible. Otherwise, the simulated impedance curve and resonance characteristics may differ significantly from the actual result. For high-speed PCB decoupling, component selection should therefore go beyond nominal capacitance. The package, effective capacitance, ESL, SRF, and—most importantly—the complete current-loop PCB layout should all be considered. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS by: Mila Sep 14,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout ESD protection esd protection circuit Previous articles have covered key technologies related to chip ESD, including ESD diodes, power clamps, CDM mechanisms, and ESD testing procedures, with a focus on chip-level electrostatic discharge protection. However, a common problem in real-world engineering applications is that an IC may pass all standard ESD tests but still suffer damage or failure when used on an actual customer circuit board. Engineers often assume that the problem is insufficient chip-level ESD protection. However, this judgment has limitations. Not all electrical failures are caused by ESD. In many real-world applications, the underlying cause may instead be EOS (Electrical Overstress). 1. What Is EOS? EOS stands for Electrical Overstress. It refers to a condition in which an IC is subjected to voltage, current, or power stress beyond its designed safe operating limits, resulting in electrical abnormalities or physical damage. Common EOS Scenarios EOS can occur in many real-world application conditions, including: Power supply overvoltage I/O input voltage exceeding the specified limit Output short circuits Hot-plugging transients Line surge events Power supply reversal Negative voltage stress Ground bounce Abnormal power sequencing EOS is not a single standardized failure test model. Instead, it is a general term for failures caused by excessive electrical stress. Any voltage, current, or power stress that exceeds the device's designed tolerance can potentially result in EOS failure. 2. Key Differences Between EOS and ESD Both ESD and EOS can cause electrical damage to an IC, which is why they are easily confused in engineering practice. However, they differ significantly in terms of stress characteristics, duration, energy, and failure mechanisms. （Comparison of ESD and EOS Waveforms） 3. Why Can an IC Fail After Passing ESD Tests? Passing standardized HBM and CDM tests only demonstrates that an IC can withstand specific short-duration electrostatic discharge stresses under defined test conditions. It does not mean that the device can withstand every type of electrical transient that may occur in a real system. Standard ESD Tests Have Limited Coverage Standard ESD tests are designed around defined test models and conditions. They verify whether an IC's ESD protection structures and discharge paths can safely handle specified electrostatic pulses. However, these tests cannot reproduce every electrical stress that may occur after the IC is integrated into a complete circuit board. Real-World Applications Introduce Different Electrical Stress In actual circuit board applications, electrical stress may come from: Cable insertion and removal Power-on overshoot External load short circuits Surge coupling through long cables Back-EMF from motors, relays, and other inductive loads Transient ground potential rise Abnormal sequencing between multiple power domains Accidental power connection Compared with standardized ESD pulses, these events may have longer durations, higher accumulated energy, or repeated stress characteristics, resulting in different types of IC damage. The internal ESD protection circuit of an IC is primarily designed to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses. Its purpose is to establish a controlled discharge path and divert transient energy. Therefore, passing ESD tests does not mean that an IC has system-level protection against all EOS conditions. （ESD Test PASS vs Real PCB FAIL） 4. The Functional Limits of Internal ESD Protection A common misconception in system design is that an IC can withstand all external electrical disturbances simply because its pins include an ESD protection circuit. In practice, this assumption can create significant reliability risks. What Is Internal ESD Protection Designed For? The internal ESD protection structure is an important protection layer against electrostatic events. It is designed to provide a low-impedance path for short-duration ESD currents and prevent excessive voltage from reaching sensitive internal circuits. However, this protection is not intended to absorb large amounts of energy for an extended period. It should therefore not be treated as a substitute for system-level EOS protection. What Happens Under Sustained Overvoltage? For example, if an I/O pin is continuously exposed to a voltage beyond its specified operating range and the internal protection structure enters conduction, current may continue to flow into or through the IC. As the stress continues, the protection device and related circuits can generate significant heat. Depending on the electrical stress and internal current path, this may eventually cause damage to components such as: I/O protection devices Output driver circuits Power clamp structures Metal interconnects Vias PN junctions Core input circuits The actual damage location depends on the magnitude and duration of the external stress as well as the current path inside the IC. Why Board-Level Protection Is Required A key engineering principle is that internal ESD protection is primarily intended to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses, while system-level electrical stress with significant energy should be limited and protected at the board level. Common board-level protection methods include: TVS devices Series current-limiting resistors Power clamps Fuses Overcurrent protection Appropriate grounding Proper PCB layout The goal is not simply to add more protection components, but to limit the voltage, current, and energy that can reach the IC and provide a controlled path for transient energy. （Board-Level Protection + IC Internal ESD Protection） 5. Typical EOS Damage Locations and Failure Analysis EOS damage is closely related to the actual current path created by the electrical stress. Different types of stress can affect different areas of the IC: Power supply overvoltage: May damage power clamp structures, internal power circuits, metal interconnects, and thin gate-oxide devices. I/O input overvoltage: May damage I/O protection structures, input circuits, pull-up or pull-down protection structures, and core gate circuits. Output short circuit: May damage output driver circuits, metal interconnects, vias, and local diffusion regions. Negative voltage stress: May damage I/O protection structures, junction regions, and input/output circuits. Therefore, EOS failure analysis should not rely solely on the appearance of a localized burn mark. It is more important to trace the source of the electrical stress, current entry and exit paths, stress duration, and energy to identify the root cause. 6. Engineering Differences Between ESD and EOS Failure Signatures There is no absolute method for distinguishing ESD from EOS based solely on physical failure signatures. However, practical failure analysis often reveals some characteristic differences that can be used as initial clues. Common ESD failure characteristics include: Localized single-point damage Gate-oxide breakdown Abnormalities around I/O protection structures Localized PN-junction leakage Leakage or parameter changes at a single pin Common EOS failure characteristics include: More obvious thermal damage Localized melting or burning of metal Significant thermal damage to vias or metal interconnects Large-area circuit damage Abnormalities along power paths Damage to output driver circuits Simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins or circuit nodes It is important to note that these failure signatures are only supporting evidence and should not be treated as final conclusions. Accurate differentiation between ESD and EOS failures requires comprehensive analysis of the failure scenario, electrical test data, application environment, test conditions, damage location, and physical analysis results. 7. The Risks of Misdiagnosing EOS as ESD In real-world applications, misdiagnosing an EOS failure as insufficient ESD protection can lead to an incorrect corrective strategy, wasting design resources while leaving the actual problem unresolved. When an IC is damaged by system-level EOS, simply increasing the size of the internal ESD protection structure, strengthening the internal power clamp, or widening internal metal interconnects generally cannot solve the system-level failure. The root cause may instead be related to board-level electrical stress, such as excessive external surge energy, improper TVS selection, continuous power supply overvoltage, load short circuits, abnormal hot-plug timing, or the lack of an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path for inductive loads. The key risk of misdiagnosing EOS is that engineers may continue to optimize the chip's ESD protection circuit without addressing the actual source and energy path of the system-level electrical stress. As a result, the same failure may occur repeatedly. Therefore, when investigating electrical failures in real-world applications, both chip-level and system-level factors should be considered rather than focusing only on the internal ESD structure. 8. Key Questions for Troubleshooting Suspected EOS Failures When an IC experiences an electrical failure, the following factors can be checked first to avoid automatically classifying the problem as an ESD failure: Failure Scenario Did the failure occur during a standard ESD test or during actual customer operation? Did it occur at the moment of power-up, during cable insertion or removal, after a load short circuit, or when a motor or relay was activated? Failure Location Is the problem limited to leakage at a single I/O pin, a low-resistance path between the power supply and ground, or simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins? Has the overall operating current of the IC changed significantly? Stress Characteristics Was the failure caused by a short-duration transient pulse, continuous overvoltage, or overcurrent? Was there any periodic or repeated electrical stress or abnormal power sequencing? Board-Level Protection Does the circuit board include TVS or other surge protection? Is an appropriate current-limiting circuit provided? Does the power supply have overvoltage or clamping protection? Does the grounding path provide sufficiently low impedance? Does the inductive load have an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path? These factors can help determine whether the failure is related to system-level EOS and provide a basis for tracing the electrical stress path into the IC. Conclusion Both ESD and EOS can cause IC leakage, short circuits, functional abnormalities, and physical damage, but their stress characteristics, protection strategies, and corrective measures are significantly different. Passing standard ESD tests only verifies the IC's ability to withstand specific short-duration electrostatic pulses and does not cover every overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, power reversal, or ground-bounce condition that may occur in a real system. Therefore, when investigating an IC failure in an actual application, engineers should not determine the root cause solely based on the fact that the device passed ESD testing or on the appearance of localized physical damage. Instead, the failure scenario, electrical stress, failure location, current path, board-level protection, and physical analysis results should be considered together. For electrical stress outside standard ESD test conditions, such as overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, and inductive load transients, EOS should be considered as a potential root cause. Appropriate board-level protection can help limit the voltage, current, and energy reaching the IC and reduce the risk of application-level failure. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity.
